before.title: Squared-loss benchmark and finite normalization
before.detail: For independent square-integrable P,Y, use the variance identity and zero covariance. Pointwise support produces L2 for the concrete learner; identical laws align the means and variances before summing. For a probability measure and measurable Y supported pointwise in [0,1], the population mean m = E[Y] belongs to [0,1], E[(m-Y)^2] = Var(Y), and Var(Y) <= E[(u-Y)^2] for every fixed real u. The preserved source_mean_optimal derives these facts from expected_square_decomposition. This identifies the fixed population benchmark; it does not compare the expectation of a random hindsight minimum or give an IID rate. Write L_T = E[sum_{t<T}(p_t-Y_t)^2] and sigma^2 = Var(Y_0). Linearity of the finite integral sum gives the IID identity. Each residual squared-error integral is nonnegative; positive T permits the exact scalar normalization. The scalar normalization lemma itself applies to any real total.
before.fallback: The generic identity consumes independence; the actual mean learner derives that premise from strict past and joint independence. Finite nonnegativity and normalization do not by themselves prove stochastic asymptotic success.

after.detail: For independent square-integrable P,Y, use the variance identity and zero covariance. Pointwise support produces L2 for the concrete learner; identical laws align the means and variances before summing. For a probability measure and measurable Y supported pointwise in [0,1], the population mean m = E[Y] belongs to [0,1], E[(m-Y)^2] = Var(Y), and Var(Y) <= E[(u-Y)^2] for every fixed real u. The preserved source_mean_optimal derives these facts from expected_square_decomposition. This identifies the fixed population benchmark; it does not compare the expectation of a random hindsight minimum or give an IID rate. Write L_T = E[sum_{t<T}(p_t-Y_t)^2] and sigma^2 = Var(Y_0). Linearity of the finite integral sum gives the IID identity. Each residual squared-error integral is nonnegative; positive T permits the exact scalar normalization. The scalar normalization lemma itself applies to any real total.
after.fallback: The generic identity consumes independence; the actual mean learner derives that premise from strict past and joint independence. Finite nonnegativity and normalization do not by themselves prove stochastic asymptotic success.

after.detail: Assume the actual predictor has finite nonpositive normalized-regret limits at every fixed comparator in [0,1]. Use comparators 0 and 1 in meanPredict_fixedRegret_limit_iff. Their squared-distance limits determine a limit for the empirical mean through the displayed identity. Bounded observations make every positive-prefix mean feasible, so its limit belongs to [0,1]. Conversely, meanPredict_limitNoRegret_of_mean_converges supplies the nonpositive limit for every real comparator and hence every unit comparator.

after.title: Construct the two cofinal empirical-mean subsequences
after.detail: Set d0=0 and d(n+1)=1-d(floor(n/2)). Strong induction on the smaller parent proves that each value is zero or one. The children at 2k+1 and 2k+2 both equal 1-dk, giving the prefix-sum recurrence for S_n=sum of d_t over t<n. Induction gives S_(4^n-1)=2(4^n-1)/3 and the corresponding low count. Divide only by the proved positive high and low horizons. Both horizons diverge, and the reciprocal correction tends to zero.

after.title: Separate best-regret convergence from fixed-comparator convergence
after.detail: The dyadic range theorem permits reuse of meanPredict_noRegret and meanPredict_bestRegret_average_tendsto_zero for this same stream and predictor. The latter result uses an actual nonnegative FTL loss gap together with the logarithmic upper bound. If fixed-zero normalized regret tended to a finite a, meanPredict_fixedRegret_limit_iff would force the squared empirical mean to tend to -a. Compose with each cofinal subsequence and use uniqueness of real limits. The resulting distinct squared limits contradict one another. Comparator zero is feasible, so the all-comparator finite-limit predicate fails as well.
